blurb: How text becomes numbers: tokenizers, embedding spaces and semantic search.

cards.title: Text to integers

steps.p: A tokenizer cuts text into subword pieces: common words stay whole, rare words split into fragments like "un" + "believ" + "able".
Each piece maps to an integer in a fixed vocabulary, typically 32,000 to 200,000 entries.
Byte-pair encoding builds the vocabulary by repeatedly merging the most frequent adjacent pair of symbols in a training corpus.

cards.aside: The model never sees letters — only these ids. That explains a surprising number of its quirks.

cards.q: As a rule of thumb for English, 1,000 tokens is about how many words?
cards.why: About 750. A token averages roughly four characters of English, or three-quarters of a word. Code, numbers and non-English text usually need more tokens per word.

cards.statement: "hello" and " hello" (with a leading space) are usually the same token.
cards.why: False. Most tokenizers fold the leading space into the token, so the two are different ids. That is why a stray trailing space in a prompt can subtly change outputs.

cards.q: Byte-pair encoding starts from individual characters or bytes and then…
options: Repeatedly merges the most frequent adjacent pair into a new token
Assigns one token per dictionary word
cards.why: Greedy merging. If "t"+"h" is most common, it becomes "th"; then perhaps "th"+"e" becomes "the". Merging stops when the vocabulary reaches its target size.

cards.title: The same sentence can cost several times more tokens in some languages than in English.
cards.detail: Tokenizers trained mostly on English split other scripts into small fragments. Studies found gaps of several-fold — and in extreme cases over 10× — meaning higher cost, slower output and less effective context for those languages.

cards.statement: Byte-level tokenizers can encode any text at all, including emoji and scripts they never saw in training.
cards.why: True. Because the base alphabet is the 256 possible bytes, anything in UTF-8 can be represented, even if it falls back to one token per byte.

cards.title: A map of meaning

steps.p: Each token id selects a row from an embedding matrix — a vector of a few thousand numbers learned during training.
Because similar tokens appear in similar contexts, training pushes their vectors close together.
Consistent offsets can encode concepts such as gender, tense or country-to-capital, so vector arithmetic sometimes works.

cards.aside: In a transformer, these starting vectors are refined by every layer into context-aware representations.

cards.q: The famous result king − man + woman ≈ queen came from which 2013 model?
cards.why: word2vec, from Mikolov and colleagues at Google. It learned word vectors by predicting nearby words, and showed that relationships appeared as consistent directions in the space.

cards.q: A vocabulary of 128,000 tokens with 4,096-dimensional embeddings needs about how many parameters for the embedding table?
cards.why: 128,000 × 4,096 ≈ 524 million. That is a noticeable slice of a small model. It is one reason vocabulary size is a real design trade-off.

cards.statement: Some LLMs reuse the input embedding matrix as their output layer.
cards.why: True — weight tying. GPT-2 did this: the same matrix maps tokens to vectors and final vectors back to token scores. It saves parameters; many larger models now keep them separate.

cards.title: Inside a transformer, "bank" gets different vectors in "river bank" and "bank loan".
cards.detail: word2vec gave each word one fixed vector. Transformers start from one, but attention quickly mixes in context, so by middle layers the two senses have separate representations.

cards.q: Cosine similarity between two vectors ranges from…
cards.why: −1 to 1. It is the cosine of the angle: 1 means the same direction, 0 orthogonal, −1 opposite. In practice text embeddings tend to cluster in the positive range.

cards.title: How semantic search works

steps.p: An embedding model turns a whole sentence or paragraph into a single vector that captures its meaning.
It learns from pairs that belong together, such as a question and its answer, pulling them close and pushing unrelated pairs apart.
At query time, the question is embedded and the nearest stored vectors are returned — matching meaning, not keywords.

cards.aside: "How do I reset my password?" can match "Recovering account access" with no words in common.

cards.statement: The embedding model used for search is usually the same model as the chat LLM.
cards.why: False. Embedding models are usually separate, much smaller encoders trained specifically for similarity. They are cheap enough to run over millions of documents.

cards.q: Vector databases often use approximate nearest-neighbor indexes like HNSW. What do they trade away?
options: A small chance of missing the true nearest match, in exchange for huge speedups
cards.why: Exactness for speed. Exact search compares the query with every vector. HNSW navigates a graph of neighbors and finds almost all true matches in a fraction of the time.

cards.title: Some embedding models let you simply chop vectors shorter and still use them.
cards.detail: "Matryoshka" training makes the first dimensions carry the most information. OpenAI's text-embedding-3 models support this, letting you cut storage several-fold for a modest accuracy cost.

cards.statement: Vectors from two different embedding models can be compared with each other directly.
cards.why: False. Each model learns its own coordinate system. Switching models means re-embedding every stored document.

cards.q: Why do many search systems combine embeddings with old-fashioned keyword search?
options: Embeddings are illegal in some countries
Keyword search catches exact names, codes and rare terms that embeddings can blur
cards.why: Complementary strengths. Embeddings handle paraphrase; keywords (like BM25) nail exact matches such as error codes or product names. Hybrid search merges both rankings.

cards.q: Why have LLMs historically struggled to count the r's in "strawberry"?
options: They see a few tokens, not individual letters
cards.why: They never see the letters. "strawberry" arrives as a couple of token ids. Spelling out letters requires the model to have memorized each token's spelling — a task it was never directly trained on.

cards.title: "SolidGoldMagikarp" was a token that made GPT-3 behave bizarrely.
cards.detail: It existed in the vocabulary (from a Reddit username) but almost never appeared in training data, so its embedding was barely trained. Asking about such "glitch tokens" produced evasions, insults or nonsense.

cards.statement: All LLM tokenizers split numbers into single digits.
cards.why: False. It varies: Llama's tokenizers split digits individually, while some OpenAI tokenizers group up to three digits per token. These choices measurably affect arithmetic ability.

cards.q: What is the main trade-off of a larger vocabulary?
options: Shorter sequences, but a bigger embedding table and more rarely-seen tokens
cards.why: Length vs size. More tokens per entry means text compresses into fewer steps, saving compute and context. The cost is more parameters and rare tokens that barely get trained.

cards.title: Meta's Llama 3 quadrupled its vocabulary from 32,000 to 128,000 tokens.
cards.detail: Meta reported this encoded the same text with up to 15% fewer tokens, which makes inference cheaper and effectively stretches the context window.

cards.title: See your text the way a model does
cards.body: Tokenizer viewers color each token in a piece of text. Ten seconds with one explains odd failures with code, numbers and names better than any article.
cards.challenge: Paste a sentence with a number and a name into an online tokenizer viewer and count where the splits land.
